_comment: Service Control Policy for the OU holding the lake and compute accounts.
The only control on this list that no principal in the account can argue with. A
permissions boundary can be lifted by whoever can edit the boundary policy; an identity
policy can be widened by whoever can attach policies; an SCP can be changed only from
the management account. Everything else in this design is a ceiling; this is the roof.
Denies the IRREVERSIBLE subset only. Terraform's convergence model destroys and recreates
as normal operation -- an immutable field change, a rename -- so a blanket deny on delete
breaks ordinary applies. What is denied here is the set that cannot be undone: a deleted
KMS key makes every object under it unreadable forever, a deleted object version removes
the undo, a stopped trail loses the record of what happened.
Attach at the OU, not the root, so the management account keeps a way back in.
Scoped to the boundary ARN. A blanket deny on iam:DeletePolicyVersion breaks every
managed-policy update once the 5-version quota is reached -- including legitimate
ones -- so the narrow form is the correct one.
The identity policy already conditions CreateRole on the boundary. Repeating it at
the OU means an account admin cannot create an unbounded role either, which is the
case the identity policy cannot reach.

Verified against this repo: modules/storage-medallion-s3/main.tf declares
aws_s3_bucket_versioning. Denying the action org-wide fails `terraform apply` on every
new bucket the primary storage module creates -- the control would break the thing it
is meant to protect, on day one, for every user.
Catch suspension detectively instead: an AWS Config rule (s3-bucket-versioning-enabled)
plus MFA Delete on the buckets that hold data. A published SCP template that quietly
breaks bucket creation is worse than no template.
s3:DeleteBucket: Terraform legitimately destroys a bucket it created -- tearing down a run workspace is
ordinary. The bucket that matters is protected by the boundary and by MFA Delete, not
by an org-wide deny that would make teardown impossible.
iam:DeleteRole: Same reasoning. A pipeline's execution role is created and destroyed with the pipeline;
the platform roles are protected by path, not by a blanket deny.
